newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-Allianz willing to wait in India.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Allianz willing to wait in India.

text.p: Allianz AG, Germany's largest insurer said on Thursday it was not in a hurry to enter the Indian market.

On Wednesday, the Indian government withdrew an insurance industry regulatory bill after failing to muster enough votes to defeat an opposition-backed amendment barring the entry of foreign firms into the huge and potentially lucrative sector.
"India as a market for insurance will be there in 20 years' time also. I am not in a hurry," Michael Diekmann, CEO, Asia Pacific, Allianz AG told Reuters in an interview.
He said it was a shame that the bill had been withdrawn. It had sent out a very bad signal to the outside world, he added, and was a major drawback for those looking for a better life.
"This decision affects investments from pharmaceutical companies and hospital firms that go hand in hand with a liberalised healthcare sector."
He said Allianz worked with several pharmaceutical and healthcare services companies all over the world and facilitated their entry into new markets.

Allianz announced a $30 million joint venture with India's Alpic Finance Ltd in May last to enter the health insurance business. Analysts estimate the premium paid by Indians will rise to $10 billion by 2000 from $5.5 billion in 1996.

Diekman said the equity holding in the venture would be finalised at a later date according to government regulations, and Allianz's entry into India would not be on the condition of majority equity in its joint venture.

"We have discussed the equity question with Alpic. Allianz normally seeks majority and management control which is natural once you bring in all the know-how. India is too large a country for us to insist on that."
Diekman said $30 million was the start-up capital of the joint venture, and the partners would inject more funds as soon as they were needed.
Allianz is looking at power and telecommunications for its investment funds to put money into, but insurance remains its first priority, Diekman said.
"It would be much easier for me to convince my boss about investing in infrastructure projects in India, if we were moving ahead in insurance," he added.
